154.s: Played a Kenton record; Bert joined for the trombone features and the poll-winning players.
154.q: Well he featured trombones. That’s why I wanted to go with that band. And he was very popular. I mean guys were poll winners in the band, like Shelly Manne and Art Pepper and all them. So I figured well let me go. Because Kai had done great on the band and Kai and I were friends. So I went with the…

154.t: Kenton did not swing: the Mankato story
154.s: Kenton stopped the band swinging one night in Minnesota.
154.q: One night we played in Mankato, Minnesota. Mankato Ballroom. And generally Stan would like spread out. But this night the bandstand was small. So we were like this. And the band started swinging. And of course we all wanted to swing. So the band was swinging and he stopped it. He said, “this is not…

154.t: Kenton's five-trombone section and Pete Rugolo
154.q: Very knowledgeable about the horns and how to write for them and all that. He’s still writing.

938.t: Kenton's place in jazz and the 1955 band
938.s: Noto and Menza discuss Kenton as an organizer and front man rather than a jazz player, the 1955 band and its arrangers and soloists.
938.q: Yeah. He was an organizer and he presented and provided a vehicle for the players and the arrangers. He knew how to find the right arrangers for his music. The Bill Holmans, the Gerry Mulligans, the Bill Russos, Bill, I mean what’s his name, Johnny—

938.t: Menza's brief stay with Kenton and Kenton's legacy
938.s: Menza quit Kenton after two nights because it did not swing; talk of ghost bands, the library and the all-star band Noto joined.
938.q: Oh no, he talked about opera and all that, he hated it man. Yeah. And yet it had a lot to do with, his concept was very much based on that classical sort of structure. But he was a sweetheart. I know I worked with the band a short time and I mean a very short time, I had left Maynard’s band to go…

943.s: Slow versus fast, and Kenton's brass-heavy band as dragging a water buffalo; Stan was a great leader.
943.q: Not really. I learned that too, when with Kenton’s band you had to push. Because Kenton’s band was like dragging a dead water buffalo through the mud. I mean it was so brass heavy you know. And I don’t say that in a disparaging way. It had its own way of swinging, it was just sort of lugubrious…

943.t: Kenton on Basie: all they do is swing
943.s: Rowe reads Sam Noto's anecdote about Stan Kenton hearing Basie, and they agree Kenton's charts were not meant to swing.
943.q: Oh of course. Of course, yeah, definitely. Yeah.

372.t: The Kenton sax section and Joe Henderson's story
372.s: They name the saxophonists and trumpeters, and Kirchner tells how Joe Henderson loved the Kenton band.
372.q: No, that was before. Tony Ferrina, and I think Gerry played a short time. I know he did with the Claude Thornhill band but I’m not sure about that.

372.t: Holman, Russo and Mulligan arrangements for Konitz
372.s: They discuss pieces by Holman and Russo, Mulligan's charts, and Mulligan's 1957 big band date.
372.q: Later. I think Bill wrote his for Bird and I recorded that. A few that he wrote for Bird: “My Funny Valentine” and something else.

49.t: Stan Kenton, Balboa Beach and playing like Earl Hines
49.s: Hazel tells of helping stranded musicians in California, seeing Kenton on piano, and challenging him about sounding like Hines.
49.q: Later, he got more frenzied as he got into another kind of music. Well, you changed like that. I've seen bands do that. I've seen bands make a national reputation playing one style. And the minute they get in the money, they changed the band around and play all together different. And it synced.…

598.s: He prefers Herman's swing to the 1948 Kenton band but loves the 1953 Kenton band with its star personnel, and discusses the Neophonic.
598.q: Well I’ve got to preface what I say here. The first time I joined Kenton was in 1948 and it was the Eager Beaver Band. I wasn’t really crazy about that band. I liked Woody’s band better when I was with the band earlier, it was more of a swinging type band. But, as I stayed with the band, ‘48 was…

592.t: Moving to Stan Kenton and his two teachers
592.s: Both bands' players lacked his writing background; he credits teachers Santy Runion and Junie Ferrell, chosen by his parents.
592.q: Oh yeah. Well actually a lot of both bands’ music were less than what I was used to because with the people that I grew up with were members of the same band — we would all be writing charts for the band and learning from each other and most of the people who were on Woody’s band or Stan’s band…

889.t: Benge trumpet, Kenton versus Basie swing
889.s: A worn Benge lead pipe, then the difference between Basie's short swinging figures and Kenton's orchestral sound.
889.q: He never had to go like that. We were out, full out, the whole time. I was playing a Benge trumpet then, Jesus, that thing, man. When I got rid of that horn and changed to something different the lead pipe and the mouthpiece holder — well there’s supposed to be a little gap as far as the mouthpiece…

352.s: Woody Herman and Stan Kenton were kind to him; Kenton wrote for Maynard Ferguson and used Bob Graettinger.
352.q: were really wonderful, Woody Herman, he was great to me. I had him on the show three times. He really was a great guy. And when we were down to West Winfield, he was playing a high school down there and don’t I go down. And I’m sitting in the audience and a guy comes up with a note and he says,…

531.t: Programs and writers: Mike Abene, Mendoza and others
531.s: The band's weekly varied programs and Michael Abene's writing for doubles have educated her ears.
531.ch: New York and the WDR Big Band
531.q: It is absolutely a thrill and it has really been also such an education for me as a musician to be immersed in all these different sounds and every week something different. A couple of weeks ago we just did a program with Vince Mendoza — he arranged Michel LeGrand’s music. Next week Bob Minter is…

834.s: Varner thinks Kenton wanted a direct sound, unlike the horn.
834.q: I think – I never thought about it much one way or the other, but I think he wanted that direct sound. He didn’t want the more non-directional. Because the thing with the horn, it’s true if there’s a big band and there’s even a couple of horns if it’s soft it’ll work. Like Claude Thornhill. But if…

913.t: Kenton's concert-orchestra vision and constant change
913.s: Kenton wanted a concert jazz orchestra rather than swing, always moving to the next sound.
913.q: And then one time they were having some discussion with some of the musicians and Stan is saying, “I got certain ideas that I want this band to do and it isn’t a matter of swing. It isn’t a matter of coming from the old big band and the dance bands. It’s a matter of being a concert jazz orchestra”…

153.t: What counts as a swing band: Glenn Miller, Artie Shaw, Stan Kenton
153.s: He explains why Miller's band wasn't a swing band, lists the true swing bands, and says Kenton only swung once Bill Holman wrote for it.
153.q: Benny told me that one day when I was talking – Benny Goodman – he said – first of all, that was the most successful band as far as making money was concerned. It was a good band. No question about it. They played well. They played dance music, a certain kind of dance music that’s just vanilla. It…

223.t: Back with Kenton and the chart Zoot
223.s: He writes a piece for Zoot Sims and Kenton says it sounds like Basie.
223.q: Yeah. I got an opportunity to write a piece for Zoot, which I called Zoot. Come to think of it, Stan did finally start announcing that piece. In his car on his way home from the rehearsal, he – back to the hotel. We were in Cincinnati – he said, “I like the Zoot piece, although it sounds a little…

328.t: Kenton versus Ferguson; using many arrangers
328.s: Hampton compares Kenton and Ferguson and praises leaders who use many arrangers, as he does.
328.ch: Maynard Ferguson and Dizzy's big band
328.q: They have things in common. They have some things that are in common. One thing that they have in common is Kenton was always playing the music of a lot of different arrangers. He never stayed with one person or with himself. He played music, and that was very smart, because you can never have all…

379.s: He says marrying American harmony and Cuban rhythm requires deep knowledge, and Kenton's band could not swing.
379.q: Well, he would (inaudible) because he would (inaudible), he said, Mario, you know, American music has progressed a whole lot harmonically, but rhythm-wise remained the same. So he was getting into this idea, do you want to (inaudible) influence this.

384.t: Russ Morgan as leader, and Venuti and Rank in later years
384.s: Morgan was a capable leader and arranger, Bill Challis became arranger, and Morehouse says Joe Venuti sounded the same over the years; Virginia met Bill Rank at festivals.
384.q: Russ Morgan was a good leader. He was a good leader.

387.s: Kirchner hears Norvo-era charts in Mulligan and Brookmeyer; Sauter recalls a chart for Gerry that was not his style.
387.q: One of them I did for Gerry and it was not his style either; he didn't want to do it. He put it away and that was it.

455.t: Stan Kenton asks for Earl Hines-style charts
455.s: Pianist Stan Kenton befriends Budd in Arnheim's band and asks for arrangements in Earl Hines's manner.
455.ch: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
